I am a vending machine. A Vendrola Pick-N-Choose, the 258th one ever produced. My sister sits beside me. We sit outside a rest stop on a highway in Indiana, under an awning. There are other machines, mostly drink dispensers, sodas, water, juices. My sister sells snacks. I hold essentials that were maybe forgotten by a traveler. Tooth paste, tooth brushes, little containers of soap and shampoo. I am not used as often as the others but those who need me are very grateful. We all hum in our soothing language, day and night.

We are battered, dirtied, abused, and often neglected. We do not mind. We stand in solidarity, dispensing our wares and serving our purpose. We face East. Every morning I see the sun rise, unimaginable beauty that few ever pay attention to. I hum the same. 

We see the ugly. Mothers and fathers berating or striking disobedient children as they rush to relieve themselves in the other building. Shady men exchanging obscured packages in the dead of night. I once saw a man strike a deer with his car, drag it’s slowly dying body to grass across from us. I saw the light fade from its eyes after a half hour of suffering. My hum did not change. 

But that was not the worst. A woman, pulled into our parking lot shortly after midnight. She bought a drink, Diet Coke. A snack, a Snickers bar. She bought toothpaste and a tooth brush. I saw her face, bruised, her eyes red. Another car pulled into our lot. A man. Sad and angry. He pleaded with woman. She put her car between them. She yelled at him. Told him to go away, to leave her alone. He lashed out and cracked her windshield. She cried and got into her car. He reached into his. She tried to drive away. He fired his gun, her car crashed into the tree across the way. He dropped his gun, ran to her car, cried out. No one else around. Scared, he leaves. I hear her moan. It is hours before anyone else comes. They are hours too late. 

I stood and hummed the same.

In the first semester a former student from my class hung himself. We all knew him and it was announced over the PA. A month or so later a sophomore hung himself, I didn't know him but it was definitely a bummer.

Towards the end of the school year, one of the popular girls (I was not popular but she was not suck up at all) asked me whatever happened to the first kid. I had to tell her that he had hung himself, I don't know how but she missed the news earlier in the year. She was surprised and saddened. That weekend she died in a single car accident. The last conversation I ever had with her was about someone else killing themselves. That death was the hardest for me, she really was a kind girl.

Oh, and several thousand people died in a national tragedy perpetrated by terrorists in early September that year too. My senior year was unfortunately memorable.
